How to use this file

When the Factory Works and the Cells Still Disappear

Part 1 covered anemia from a production failure — the marrow could not build enough cells. This file is the other half of the tree: the marrow builds them perfectly well and something destroys them early. The preference stated out loud in lecture: I like this one better than the one I just did.

Abbreviations used in this sectionRBC red blood cell, also called an erythrocyte · HS hereditary spherocytosis · G6PD glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase — a red cell enzyme that protects against oxidant damage · NADPH nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (reduced form) — the reducing power G6PD generates · Hb / Hgb hemoglobin. HbA = normal adult hemoglobin, HbF = fetal, HbS = sickle, HbH = the beta-4 tetramer · SCD sickle cell disease · MCV mean corpuscular volume — average red cell size · MCHC mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration — hemoglobin per unit cell volume · LDH lactate dehydrogenase — released when cells are destroyed · HPLC high performance liquid chromatography — separates hemoglobins for identification · RES reticuloendothelial system — the macrophage network of spleen, liver and marrow
🔑 Where we are on the classification tree

Same slide the lecture kept returning to. This file lives entirely inside the middle branch:

  • Blood loss — Part 1
  • Impaired red cell production — Part 1
  • Increased rate of destruction (hemolytic anemia) — this file
    • Intrinsic — membrane (hereditary spherocytosis), enzyme (G6PD deficiency), deficient globin chains (thalassemia), structurally abnormal globin chains (sickle cell disease)
    • Extrinsic — antibody-mediated destruction, mechanical trauma (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia), hypersplenism
🧠 The one organ that appears in every single disease in this file

The spleen. The lecture personified it deliberately, and it is worth adopting: the spleen is the cleaner. It patrols for red cells that are the wrong shape, the wrong stiffness, or coated in something they should not be, and it removes them. It is doing its job correctly in every disease below — the problem is that the body keeps producing defective cells for it to find.

  • Spherocytosis — the cell is a ball instead of a disc → the spleen removes it.
  • G6PD deficiency — oxidized hemoglobin precipitates as a Heinz body → the spleen bites the inclusion out.
  • Thalassemia — unpaired globin chains precipitate → the spleen removes the cell.
  • Sickle cell disease — the cell is rigid and misshapen → the spleen removes it, until the spleen itself infarcts.

Three consequences follow everywhere: splenomegaly, jaundice from heme breakdown, and pigmented gallstones from chronic bilirubin load.

Anemia II LO 1

Anemia part 2 · objective 1

Hemolysis — Intravascular versus Extravascular

One question decides the entire laboratory workup: where was the red cell destroyed? Inside the blood vessel, or outside it. The two produce genuinely different laboratory signatures, and one of them can kill a kidney.

🔑 What normal red cell turnover looks like

A red cell lives about 120 days — roughly four months. At the end of that it is cleared by the spleen, and its hemoglobin is recycled. A cartoon shown in lecture has the spleen saying “Well done, red blood cell, you have lived honorably” and the cell protesting “Lived? I am only four months old” as it is thrown away. That is normal. Hemolysis is when it happens far too early.

🔑 All hemolytic anemias share three features
  1. Shortening of red cell lifespanThe defining event — cells are destroyed before their 120 days are up.
  2. Accumulation of the products of hemoglobin catabolismChiefly bilirubin, which is unconjugated (indirect) because it has not yet reached the liver. This is what makes patients jaundiced.
  3. Compensatory increase in erythropoiesis within the bone marrowThe marrow senses the loss and turns the factory up. This is why the reticulocyte count is HIGH and the marrow is hypercellular — the single cleanest split from everything in Part 1.

Intravascular versus extravascular hemolysis — two different destinations for the same hemoglobin.

🩸

Intravascular — destroyed inside the vessel

The cell ruptures in the circulation, spilling free hemoglobin directly into the plasma.

  • Schistocytes (sometimes) — fragmented red cells, literally torn up
  • Hemoglobinemia — free hemoglobin in plasma. Spun plasma looks pink or red instead of yellow
  • Hemoglobinuria — hemoglobin spilling into the urine, which looks dark or tea-coloured
  • Jaundice — unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia
  • Decreased or ABSENT haptoglobin — the most sensitive marker
🫀

Extravascular — destroyed outside the vessel

The cell is removed intact by a splenic macrophage, which dismantles the hemoglobin internally. Nothing free is released into the plasma.

  • Spherocytes — the classic morphology, from partial membrane removal
  • Decreased haptoglobin, but only mildly — some hemoglobin still leaks
  • Jaundice — unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia
  • Splenomegaly — the spleen enlarges from the work
  • No hemoglobinemia or hemoglobinuria
🧠 Haptoglobin — nature's mop

Haptoglobin is a plasma protein whose only job is to bind free hemoglobin released after intravascular hemolysis. The haptoglobin–hemoglobin complex is then cleared by the reticuloendothelial system, and because it is consumed in the process, the serum haptoglobin falls.

The useful framing: free heme in the plasma is so dangerous that evolution built a dedicated scavenger for it. So a low or absent haptoglobin means the mop has been used. It is a consumption marker, not a production marker — which is exactly why it falls further in intravascular hemolysis, where there is far more free hemoglobin to mop up.

⚠️ Why intravascular hemolysis is the more dangerous one

Hemoglobin is essential — inside a red cell. Free in the plasma it is toxic, and specifically toxic to the kidney. Free heme filtered at the glomerulus causes tubular injury and acute kidney injury. This is the mechanism behind the deaths from ABO-incompatible transfusion that are covered in the transfusion lecture.

The one-line summary: extravascular hemolysis is bad; intravascular hemolysis is worse.

🪝 Memory hook — Pink plasma, dark urine, no haptoglobin — the intravascular triad

You can make the call at the bench. Spin a tube: yellow plasma is normal, pink plasma is free hemoglobin. Then look at the urine — dark or tea-coloured is hemoglobinuria. Then check the haptoglobin, which will be absent, not merely low.

Extravascular hemolysis gives you none of those three. It gives you spherocytes on the smear and a big spleen instead.

MarkerIntravascularExtravascularWhy
Plasma appearancePink / redYellow (normal)Free hemoglobin only reaches plasma when the cell bursts in the vessel
HaptoglobinVery low or absentMildly decreasedConsumed clearing free hemoglobin
HemoglobinuriaPresentAbsentOnly free plasma hemoglobin is filtered
Characteristic cellSchistocytes (fragments)Spherocytes (balls)Shearing versus partial membrane removal
Unconjugated bilirubinRaisedRaisedHeme is broken down either way
Lactate dehydrogenaseRaisedRaisedReleased from destroyed cells
Reticulocyte countRaisedRaisedMarrow compensating — this is the split from Part 1
Spleen sizeUsually normalEnlargedThe spleen is doing the destroying
Kidney riskHigh — free heme is nephrotoxicLowThe reason intravascular is worse

Q: A patient's spun plasma is pink, urine dipstick is positive for blood but microscopy shows no red cells, and haptoglobin is undetectable. What kind of hemolysis is this, and what organ is at immediate risk?

Answer

Intravascular hemolysis. The pink plasma is hemoglobinemia; a dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy is hemoglobinuria — the dipstick detects heme, not intact cells. The undetectable haptoglobin means the scavenger has been completely consumed. The organ at immediate risk is the kidney: filtered free heme causes tubular injury and acute kidney injury.

Q: Why is the reticulocyte count HIGH in hemolytic anemia but LOW in iron deficiency, B12 deficiency and anemia of chronic disease?

Answer

Because the marrow is intact in hemolysis. The third shared feature of every hemolytic anemia is a compensatory increase in erythropoiesis — cells are being destroyed peripherally, the marrow detects the loss and works harder, so it releases more immature cells. In the Part 1 anemias, the marrow itself is the problem (missing raw material, or suppressed by inflammation), so it cannot respond and the reticulocyte count stays low. One cheap test splits the classification tree in half.

Anemia part 2 · membrane disorder

Hereditary Spherocytosis — a Broken Cytoskeleton

The first of four inherited red cell defects. The cell is built with a faulty scaffold, loses its disc shape, and the spleen — doing exactly what it is supposed to do — removes it.

🔑 The genetics and the defect
  • Autosomal dominant genetic condition.
  • An intrinsic defect in the red cell membrane that renders erythrocytes spheroidal rather than the normal biconcave disc.
  • The proteins involved are cytoskeletal: ankyrin, band 3, β-spectrin, α-spectrin, or protein 4.2.
  • Corresponding genes on testing: ANK1, SPTB, SLC4A1.
  • Almost always diagnosed in childhood — these patients keep a hematologist alongside their primary care physician for life.

The normal cytoskeleton — a protein lattice that holds the biconcave shape.

Spherocytes — round, dense, and missing the central pale zone.

🧠 Why losing the scaffold costs you the shape, and the shape costs you your life

The biconcave disc is held by an internal protein lattice — a cytoskeleton clipped to the inner membrane. When one of those proteins is defective, the lattice cannot maintain the shape and the cell rounds up into a sphere. The image to hold: it stops being a doughnut and becomes a baseball.

The consequence is mechanical. A sphere has the smallest possible surface area for its volume, so it is far less deformable. A normal red cell folds itself through capillaries and through the narrow slits of the splenic cords; a spherocyte cannot. It gets stuck, the spleen identifies it as abnormal, and it is removed. This is extravascular hemolysis by definition.

What it does to the patient

Splenomegaly in hereditary spherocytosis — the spleen enlarges because it is working constantly.

🩺

Signs and symptoms

  • Anemia
  • Jaundice — unconjugated bilirubin from constant heme breakdown
  • Enlarged spleen — from the workload
  • Pigmented gallstones — chronic bilirubin load precipitates in the gallbladder
🔬

Other findings

  • Hypercellular marrow — the compensatory drive is permanently turned up
  • Hemosiderosis — iron overload, secondary to repeated transfusions
  • High MCHC — the cell is smaller for its hemoglobin content, so the concentration rises
  • High reticulocyte count — a working marrow, compensating
🪝 Memory hook — Anemia · Jaundice · Big spleen · Gallstones — the chronic extravascular quartet

Those four together are the signature of any long-standing extravascular hemolysis, not just spherocytosis. If a vignette gives you a young patient with lifelong intermittent jaundice, an enlarged spleen, and gallstones at an unusually young age, you are being shown chronic hemolysis and asked to name the mechanism.

And the gallstones are the giveaway detail: a teenager with pigmented gallstones almost never has ordinary gallbladder disease.

The two crises

🧠 How a compensated patient falls off the tightrope

The steady state was described precisely: the patient is balanced. The spleen is running in overdrive, the marrow is running in overdrive, and the two cancel out. Then something tips it.

🔥

Hemolytic crisis

Often elicited by infection — the destruction rate accelerates past what the marrow can match.

  • Significant hemolysis
  • Fever
  • Abdominal pain
  • Worsening jaundice
  • Shock in the worst events
🛑

Aplastic crisis

Suppression of red cell production, usually triggered by parvovirus B19 infection.

  • Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid precursors and shuts erythropoiesis down.
  • The image to hold: the foundation is cut out from under the compensatory drive and the patient collapses.
  • A healthy person tolerates a brief pause in red cell production. Someone whose survival depends on a marrow running at maximum does not.
⚠️ Parvovirus B19 will appear in three separate diseases in this file

Hereditary spherocytosis, and again in sickle cell disease. The mechanism is identical each time: parvovirus B19 infects red cell precursors and stops erythropoiesis. Any patient with chronic hemolysis is living on a maximally compensating marrow, so removing that compensation for even a week produces a sudden, severe drop in hemoglobin. A sudden crash in hemoglobin with a LOW reticulocyte count in a chronic hemolytic patient is an aplastic crisis until proven otherwise.

Treatment

🚑

Acute

  • Red blood cell transfusion
  • Supportive care
  • Folic acid — high red cell turnover consumes folate, and the marrow needs it to keep building
🗓️

Longer term

  • Some patients benefit from surgical removal of part or all of the spleen — take away the destroyer and the cells survive.
  • The other reason: a chronically enlarged spleen is at risk of rupture, and a ruptured spleen can be fatal because it is essentially a bag of blood.
  • The trade-off is permanent: an asplenic patient is at lifelong risk from encapsulated organisms and needs vaccination and, in children, antibiotic prophylaxis.
  • Hereditary spherocytosis is a lifelong condition. Symptoms are managed, not cured.

Laboratory diagnosis

Test or findingResult
Blood smearSpherocytes
Osmotic fragility testIncreased
Spleen sizeEnlarged
GallstonesMay be present, pigmented
ReticulocytesIncreased
Genetic testPositive for a mutation in ANK1, SPTB, or SLC4A1
Direct Coombs testNEGATIVE — this is the test that excludes autoimmune hemolysis, which also produces spherocytes
🩺 The osmotic fragility test — old-fashioned, but the logic is clean

Red cells are exposed to hypotonic saline. Water moves into the cell along its osmotic gradient, and the cell swells.

  • A normal biconcave disc has spare membrane relative to its volume — it can swell substantially into a sphere before it bursts.
  • A spherocyte is already a sphere. It has no spare surface area at all, so a small amount of swelling ruptures it.
  • Result: spheroid red cells lyse where normal cells do not — increased osmotic fragility.

An aside from lecture — I do not know why we keep teaching about old-fashioned things — is fair, but the test earns its place because the reasoning is the disease.

⚠️ Spherocytes are not specific — always send a Coombs test

Spherocytes appear in two quite different diseases: hereditary spherocytosis and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, where antibody-coated cells have membrane bitten away by splenic macrophages. The direct Coombs test separates them — negative in hereditary spherocytosis, positive in autoimmune hemolysis. Note that the case at the end of this file states the Coombs test is negative for exactly this reason.

Q: A 9-year-old with known hereditary spherocytosis presents pale and lethargic five days into a viral illness. Hemoglobin has fallen from her baseline 10.5 to 4.2 g/dL. Her reticulocyte count is 0.2%. What has happened?

Answer

An aplastic crisis, almost certainly caused by parvovirus B19. The discriminating value is the low reticulocyte count. In a hemolytic crisis the marrow would be driven harder and reticulocytes would be high; here erythropoiesis has been shut off at the precursor level. Because her survival depends on a permanently maximal marrow, losing that compensation for a few days causes a precipitous drop. Management is transfusion and supportive care until marrow function recovers.

Q: Why does splenectomy help in hereditary spherocytosis even though it does not fix the membrane defect?

Answer

Because the spleen is the site of destruction, not the site of the defect. The cells remain spherocytic after splenectomy — you can still see them on the smear — but without the splenic cords to trap and remove them, their lifespan approaches normal and the anemia resolves. It also removes the risk of splenic rupture from chronic enlargement. The permanent cost is susceptibility to encapsulated organisms, requiring vaccination against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus influenzae type b.

Anemia part 2 · enzyme deficiency

G6PD Deficiency — When the Antioxidant Defense Runs Out

The world's most common enzyme deficiency, present in over 400 million people. Most of the time it causes nothing at all — until an oxidant arrives.

🔑 The defect is instability, not absence

This is the subtlety that makes the disease make sense. The enzyme is synthesized in normal amounts. But because of the genetic variant it is unstable, with a short half-life, so activity decays as the cell ages.

The consequence: a marked deficiency in OLDER red cells, while younger cells are still protected. That single fact explains the disease's entire behaviour — why hemolysis is episodic, why it is self-limited, and why the diagnostic test can be falsely normal.

Inheritance is X-linked, so it is expressed most fully in males.

The pathway G6PD protects — NADPH regenerates glutathione, glutathione neutralizes hydrogen peroxide.

🧠 Follow the chain — four links, and G6PD is the first
  1. G6PD makes NADPHGlucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase converts glucose-6-phosphate to phosphogluconolactone, generating NADPH as it goes. In a red cell, this is the only meaningful source of NADPH.
  2. NADPH regenerates glutathioneNADPH powers glutathione reductase, which converts oxidized glutathione back to reduced glutathione.
  3. Reduced glutathione neutralizes peroxideIt converts hydrogen peroxide to water, the actual detoxifying step.
  4. Without the chain, peroxide accumulatesHydrogen peroxide builds up and oxidizes hemoglobin. Oxidized hemoglobin denatures and precipitates inside the cell as a Heinz body.
🪝 Memory hook — A red cell has no nucleus, no mitochondria, and one antioxidant plan

Every other cell in the body has alternative routes to NADPH and can make replacement protein when an enzyme wears out. A red cell can do neither — it ejected its nucleus and mitochondria on the way out of the marrow. G6PD is the whole plan. Take it away and the cell has no backup and no way to build more, which is why the enzyme's instability over the cell's lifetime is the entire disease.

What the spleen does about it

Bite cells and blister cells — the fingerprints of a splenic macrophage removing a Heinz body.

  1. Hemoglobin is oxidized and precipitatesThe denatured hemoglobin forms an inclusion — a Heinz body — stuck to the inner membrane. Heinz bodies need a supravital stain (crystal violet) to see; they do not show on a routine smear.
  2. The spleen finds itA splenic macrophage detects the abnormal inclusion. Put another way: the spleen goes ‘that thing is wrong’ and takes a bite out of it.
  3. Bite cells and blister cells resultThe macrophage physically removes the inclusion plus the overlying membrane, leaving a bite cell — a red cell with a semicircular chunk missing. A blister cell is the same event with the membrane still stretched over the defect, like a blister.
  4. Less damaged cells become spherocytesIf the cell loses membrane but survives, it loses deformability and recalibrates into a spherocyte — which is why spherocytes are not unique to hereditary spherocytosis.

Severity — the WHO classes

WHO classification of G6PD variants. Only two classes cause clinically significant hemolysis.

ClassDeficiencyEnzyme activityClinical picture
ISevere< 10% of normalUncommon. Occurs across populations. Causes chronic hemolytic anemia — these red cells are permanently disabled
IISevere< 10% of normalMore common in Asian and Mediterranean populations. Intermittent hemolysis. This is G6PD Mediterranean — half-life measured in hours, so the entire red cell population is susceptible and hemolysis can be severe
IIIModerate10–60% of normal10% of Black males in the United States. Intermittent hemolysis, usually with infection or drugs. This is G6PD A− — half-life about 13 days versus a normal 62, so only older cells are vulnerable and hemolysis is mild and self-limited
IVMild to noneNormal to mildly increasedRare. No hemolysis
VNone — more activity> 150% of normalRare. No clinical significance
🔑 Only two variants matter clinically
  • G6PD A− (WHO class III) — seen in about 10% of American Black males. Half-life moderately reduced (13 days versus a normal 62), so hemolysis is mild and limited to older, deficient red cells and stops on its own.
  • G6PD Mediterranean (WHO class II) — prevalent in the Middle East. Markedly abnormal, with a half-life measured in hours. The entire red cell population is susceptible, so hemolysis can be severe.

Global distribution — and why it exists at all

Global distribution of G6PD deficiency — overlay a malaria map and they are the same picture.

🧬 The malaria hypothesis — and the pattern to notice
  • G6PD deficiency is the world's most common enzyme deficiency, affecting over 400 million people.
  • Highest prevalence in the tropical and subtropical Eastern Hemisphere: Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia.
  • The distribution is linked to populations historically exposed to endemic malaria — the deficiency provides a protective advantage against severe Plasmodium falciparum, though it is not fully protective.

The lecture flagged this as one of the things most most fascinating in medicine, and it recurs later in this file with sickle cell trait: a mutation that was advantageous in the heterozygous state under malaria pressure becomes a disease when you inherit too much of it. Note also the caution — the geography reflects where genes are common, not a reason to reason about individual patients by ancestry.

What triggers a crisis

1

Infections

Viral hepatitis, pneumonia, and typhoid fever. In practice this is the commonest trigger of all — and it is why a hemolytic episode is so often mistaken for the infection worsening.

2

Drugs

Antimalarials — primaquine and chloroquine; sulfonamides; nitrofurantoin. Note the irony: the drugs used against the disease G6PD deficiency evolved to resist.

3

Foods — fava beans

Fava beans generate oxidants when metabolized. This was a board question a generation ago, and in all own training and expects it still is. Favism matters because fava beans are endemic in the Mediterranean, the Middle East, and parts of Africa — exactly where the deficiency is common.

🪝 Memory hook — “Fava beans, sulfa drugs, antimalarials, and infection”

Four triggers, one mechanism: anything that raises oxidant stress. If the vignette mentions a patient of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, African or Southeast Asian ancestry who becomes acutely jaundiced and anemic days after starting an antimalarial, taking a sulfa antibiotic, eating fava beans, or developing an infection, the answer is G6PD deficiency.

And remember the shape of the attack: episodic, self-limited, because once the old cells are gone the young ones — full of fresh enzyme — survive.

Laboratory diagnosis

Test or findingResult
Blood smearBite cells, blister cells, Heinz bodies (Heinz bodies require a supravital stain)
G6PD enzyme assayDecreased
Genetic testG6PD gene mutation — X-linked
Haptoglobin, bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, reticulocytesThe usual hemolysis panel: haptoglobin low, indirect bilirubin high, LDH high, reticulocytes high
⚠️ The enzyme assay can be falsely NORMAL during an acute crisis

This follows directly from the mechanism, and it is a favourite exam point. During hemolysis the oldest, most enzyme-depleted cells are exactly the ones being destroyed, and the marrow floods the blood with reticulocytes, which have the HIGHEST enzyme levels of any red cell. Measure the average at that moment and it can look normal.

Repeat the assay two to three months after the episode, once the age distribution of the red cell population has returned to baseline. A genetic test is unaffected by timing.

Q: A 6-year-old boy of Greek ancestry develops jaundice, dark urine and pallor two days after eating fava beans at a family meal. His hemoglobin has fallen to 6.8 g/dL. A G6PD assay sent during the admission returns normal. What is the diagnosis, and why was the test normal?

Answer

G6PD deficiency — almost certainly the Mediterranean variant (WHO class II), given his ancestry and the severity. The assay was falsely normal because it was drawn during the crisis: the old, enzyme-depleted cells had already been destroyed, and the marrow's compensatory reticulocytosis flooded the sample with young cells carrying the highest enzyme levels. The assay must be repeated two to three months later, or a genetic test sent instead. The smear during the episode would show bite cells and blister cells.

Q: Why does hemolysis in G6PD A− stop on its own after a few days, while G6PD Mediterranean can cause severe, ongoing hemolysis?

Answer

It comes down to enzyme half-life. In G6PD A− (class III) the half-life is about 13 days versus a normal 62, so only the oldest cells are enzyme-depleted. Once those are destroyed, the remaining younger population still has enough enzyme and hemolysis is self-limited. In G6PD Mediterranean (class II) the half-life is measured in hours, so essentially the entire red cell population is deficient — including young cells — and hemolysis can be severe and sustained.

Anemia part 2 · deficient globin chain synthesis

Thalassemia — Not Enough of One Chain

Spherocytosis breaks the container and G6PD breaks the defenses. Thalassemia breaks the quantity of hemoglobin — you make structurally normal globin, just not enough of one kind. The damage comes from the chain you make too much of.

🔑 What thalassemia is
  • A genetic blood disorder involving less than normal amounts of hemoglobin — a production problem, not a structural one.
  • Less oxygen-carrying hemoglobin and fewer red blood cells than normal.
  • Symptoms: fatigue, weakness, paleness, and slow growth. Because it presents in childhood, failure to thrive and delayed milestones are often the first sign.
  • Mild forms may need no treatment. Severe forms require blood transfusions or a donor stem cell transplant.

The hemoglobin molecule and its genes

Four alpha genes on chromosome 16, two beta genes on chromosome 11 — the asymmetry that drives everything.

🧠 Count the genes — this is the whole framework
  • Adult hemoglobin (HbA) is α₂β₂ — two alpha chains and two beta chains.
  • You have FOUR alpha globin genes (two on each copy of chromosome 16).
  • You have TWO beta globin genes (one on each copy of chromosome 11).
  • Beta thalassemia = deficient synthesis of the beta chain.
  • Alpha thalassemia = deficient synthesis of the alpha chain.

The question put to the class: which is easier to become severely affected by? You only have two betas — lose one and you are in trouble. You have four alphas — losing one barely registers. That single asymmetry is why alpha thalassemia has four clinical grades and beta thalassemia has essentially two.

The globin switch — why fetal hemoglobin matters

The globin switch — and the two abnormal tetramers that form when a partner chain is missing.

🧠 Why a fetus needs a different hemoglobin

The lecture paused to reason this out, and it is worth reproducing. A fetus gets its oxygen from its mother, across the placenta. The mother has ordinary adult hemoglobin. For the fetus to pull oxygen off maternal hemoglobin, fetal hemoglobin must have a higher affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin does.

  • Prenatal: gamma (γ) chains pair with alpha to make HbF = α₂γ₂ — F for fetus.
  • After birth: the globin switch — gamma production falls off and beta takes over, giving HbA = α₂β₂.

This matters for three separate things later: it explains why beta thalassemia does not present at birth (the baby is still running on HbF), it explains the two abnormal tetramers below, and it explains why hydroxyurea works in sickle cell disease by turning HbF back on.

TetramerCompositionWhen it formsConsequence
HbAα₂β₂Normal adultNormal oxygen delivery
HbFα₂γ₂Normal fetusHigh oxygen affinity — correct for pulling oxygen across the placenta
HbHβ₄ — four betas, no alpha partnerAlpha thalassemia with only one working alpha geneUnstable; oxidized and precipitates as red cell inclusions, removed by the spleen
Hb Bartsγ₄ — four gammas, no alpha partnerAlpha thalassemia with no working alpha genes, in a fetusExtremely high oxygen affinity — it binds oxygen and will not let go, so it cannot deliver oxygen to tissue

The mechanism of damage

Thalassemia smear — hypochromia, variation in size and shape, and target cells.

🔑 Two hits from one problem
  1. Not enough hemoglobin → hypochromiaReduced globin synthesis means low intracellular hemoglobin, which shows as hypochromia and microcytosis — the same appearance as iron deficiency, from a completely different cause.
  2. Relative excess of the unpartnered chain → destructionThis is the part that does the real damage. If beta chains are deficient, you have a relative excess of alpha chains with nothing to pair with. These excess normal chains aggregate into insoluble complexes inside the red cell and its precursors.
  3. Precursors die in the marrowThose aggregates destroy developing cells before release — ineffective hematopoiesis. This is why the marrow is hypercellular and yet the patient is profoundly anemic.
  4. Mature cells are destroyed in the spleenAnd the ones that make it out carry inclusions the spleen finds and removes — hemolysis. Hence the classification under increased destruction.
🪝 Memory hook — The unpaired partner is the poison

The intuitive assumption is that thalassemia hurts because you make too little hemoglobin. That is only half of it, and the milder half. The severity tracks the chain you have too MUCH of. Unpartnered globin chains precipitate, damage membranes, and kill cells in the marrow and the spleen.

This is also why beta thalassemia is worse than alpha thalassemia of comparable gene loss: free alpha chains are far more unstable and damaging than free beta chains, which can at least assemble into HbH.

Alpha thalassemia — four grades

Alpha thalassemia inheritance — two trait parents, four possible outcomes.

DiagnosisGenes presentClinical picture
Silent carrier3 of 4 alpha genesBecause three normal genes remain, these individuals are completely asymptomatic and do not have anemia. The point made in lecture: more than one person in a lecture hall has this and will never know.
Alpha thalassemia trait2 of 4Mild deficiency in alpha chain synthesis. Minimal anemia and no abnormal physical signs. Microcytic with normal iron studies — the reason to check iron studies before treating a microcytic anemia with iron.
Hemoglobin H disease1 of 4Alpha chain synthesis markedly reduced, with excess beta chains forming tetramers called hemoglobin H (β₄). HbH is oxidized and visible as red cell inclusions on the smear, cannot withstand oxidative stress, precipitates, and is removed by the spleen — moderately severe anemia.
Hydrops fetalis0 of 4The most severe form. In the fetus, excess gamma chains form hemoglobin Barts (γ₄), which has extremely high oxygen affinity and therefore cannot deliver oxygen to tissue. Result: severe anoxia and intrauterine fetal death without prenatal intervention.
🩺 Which two do you actually meet in clinic?

The middle two. Silent carriers are never identified, and hydrops fetalis does not survive to become a patient without in-utero intervention. So the clinically relevant alpha thalassemias are alpha thalassemia trait — which matters mainly because it is mistaken for iron deficiency — and hemoglobin H disease.

Beta thalassemia — two mutation types, two clinical grades

Beta thalassemia inheritance from two carrier parents.

0️⃣

β⁰ thalassemia

Complete absence of beta globin chain production. No beta chains at all from that gene.

➕

β⁺ thalassemia

Reduced, but not absent, production of beta globin chains. Some output survives.

DiagnosisGenotypeClinical
Thalassemia minor (trait)Heterozygous — one normal beta gene presentMild anemia. Often mistaken for iron deficiency; iron studies are normal
Thalassemia majorHomozygous β⁰ or β⁺Severe, transfusion-dependent anemia. Presents in infancy once the globin switch removes HbF
🧠 Why beta thalassemia major presents at 6 months, not at birth

A crucial detail the globin switch explains. A fetus and a newborn run on HbF (α₂γ₂), which does not require beta chains at all. So a baby with beta thalassemia major is born completely well. Only as gamma production falls off and beta is supposed to take over — around 3 to 6 months of age — does the anemia appear.

That is exactly the history in Case 2 at the end of this file: born full-term without complications, and pallor beginning at around six months.

Treatment

1

Mild forms

Usually no treatment required.

2

Moderate forms

Regular blood transfusions as needed, iron chelation therapy to remove excess iron, and folic acid supplementation.

3

Severe (beta thalassemia major)

Lifelong transfusions every 2–4 weeks — entirely transfusion dependent. Plus iron chelation, and for cure: gene therapy or stem cell transplant. Medications to improve red cell production are also available.

⚠️ Iron overload — treating the treatment

A point made with some feeling in lecture. Transfused blood carries iron, and the human body has no physiologic mechanism to excrete iron. A patient transfused every two to four weeks for life accumulates it relentlessly, damaging heart, liver and endocrine organs.

So they must take iron chelation therapy — in the lecture's phrase, pills which treat you for the treatment. And note the irony that closes the loop with Part 1: this is the one anemia where you must remove iron rather than give it.

🩺 Gene therapy and stem cell transplant — real, and still an ordeal

Both are genuinely curative options now. But The lecture was careful not to oversell them: stem cell transplant is a very wrought treatment that can cause significant problems of its own — you are trading one disease for another. Gene therapy is performed at centres like this and is remarkable, but the patient still needs chemotherapy conditioning and still passes through a period with no functioning immune system.

Diagnosis

Hemoglobin electrophoresis — beta thalassemia shows an enlarged HbF band because beta chains are missing.

🧠 How gel electrophoresis works, and what you are looking at

The sample is loaded into a gelatinous slab and an electric current is applied. The hemoglobin species separate according to charge and molecular weight, producing discrete bands you read directly. HPLC (high performance liquid chromatography) does the same job by a different physical principle and is now more common.

In beta thalassemia the finding is an enlarged HbF band — because beta chains are deficient, the patient continues making fetal hemoglobin well past infancy. HbA₂ (α₂δ₂) is also raised.

Target cells (codocytes) — the bull's-eye appearance.

🔑 Target cells — why they look like that
  • Also called codocytes.
  • They arise from an imbalance between the cell membrane and its hemoglobin content, giving an increased surface-area-to-volume ratio — too much membrane for too little hemoglobin.
  • The imbalance is caused by the accumulation of unpaired globin chains, which form inclusions that damage the membrane and cause premature destruction.
  • The bull's-eye appearance results from hemoglobin clustering around the periphery and in the centre, separated by a pale ring.

The plainer version: there is too much membrane flopping around without enough hemoglobin to fill it, so it piles up in the middle.

Test or findingResult in thalassemia
Blood smearHypochromic (pale) red cells; anisopoikilocytosis (variation in size and shape); target cells; Heinz bodies; nucleated red cells sometimes
Mean corpuscular volumeLow — microcytic
Gel electrophoresis or HPLCAbnormal pattern; in beta thalassemia an enlarged HbF band and raised HbA₂
Genetic testingHBA1 (alpha) and HBB (beta) genes
Iron studiesMay be normal — the point is to rule out iron deficiency. May be elevated if the patient has been heavily transfused
Newborn screening (HPLC or isoelectric focusing)Elevated Hb Barts indicates alpha thalassemia; changes in HbA and HbF suggest beta thalassemia
🩺 Newborn screening is how this is actually found

Every baby born in the United States receives a newborn screen — a panel for rare but actionable conditions. Note that each state runs a different panel, which is arguably unfortunate.

The logic is the point: detect it at birth and you can put that patient on a pathway that saves their life; miss it and they are in real trouble. The pediatrician receives a positive screen and refers to a specialist center for confirmatory electrophoresis. Such centres diagnose new babies with sickle cell disease and thalassemia every week.

Q: A 2-year-old has a microcytic anemia with a mean corpuscular volume of 65 fL. His serum ferritin is 180 ng/mL and transferrin saturation is normal. His red cell count is high for the degree of anemia. What should you NOT do, and what test do you order?

Answer

Do not give iron. The completely normal iron studies with a disproportionately small MCV and a high red cell count point to thalassemia, not iron deficiency — and giving iron to a thalassemic patient achieves nothing except iron overload, which is the very thing you spend the rest of their care chelating out. Order hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC, which will show an enlarged HbF band and raised HbA₂ in beta thalassemia.

Q: Explain why hydrops fetalis is incompatible with life while hemoglobin H disease is survivable, even though both are alpha thalassemias.

Answer

It is about which tetramer forms and how it behaves. In hemoglobin H disease (one alpha gene) excess beta chains form HbH (β₄), which is unstable and precipitates — causing a moderately severe hemolytic anemia, but the patient still has some normal HbA and can deliver oxygen. In hydrops fetalis (no alpha genes) no alpha-containing hemoglobin can be made at all; excess gamma chains form Hb Barts (γ₄), which has extremely high oxygen affinity — it binds oxygen and will not release it to tissue. The fetus is profoundly anoxic despite being full of hemoglobin, causing intrauterine fetal death.

Anemia part 2 · structurally abnormal globin chains

Sickle Cell Disease — One Amino Acid

Thalassemia is a quantity problem — normal chains, not enough of them. Sickle cell disease is a quality problem: you make the right amount of beta globin, and one amino acid in it is wrong. The verdict from lecture, said plainly: it is a terrible disease.

🔑 The mutation
  • A point mutation in the beta globin chain: a single adenine-to-thymine substitution changes the 6th codon of the mature protein.
  • The result is valine substituted for glutamic acid at that position. (The lecture slide writes this as glutamine; the standard biochemistry is glutamic acid → valine.)
  • The product is hemoglobin S (HbS), which has abnormal physicochemical properties.
  • The gene is HBB — the same gene as beta thalassemia, different kind of mutation.

One nucleotide, one amino acid — and a hydrophobic valine that makes hemoglobin molecules stick to each other.

🧠 Why one hydrophobic residue does this much damage

Glutamic acid is charged and water-loving; valine is hydrophobic. Putting a hydrophobic patch on the outside of a hemoglobin molecule gives it a sticky spot, and hydrophobic patches find each other.

  1. Oxygenated, nothing happensWith oxygen bound, the molecule's conformation keeps the sticky patch tucked away. HbS behaves essentially normally.
  2. Deoxygenated, it polymerizesOn releasing oxygen the conformation shifts, the hydrophobic valine is exposed, and HbS molecules polymerize into long rigid fibers.
  3. The fibers deform the cellThose fibers distort the red cell into the sickle shape and, critically, make it inflexible.
  4. Inflexible cells get stuckA normal red cell folds through capillaries narrower than itself. A sickled cell cannot — it lodges in the microvasculature.

The class was asked what happens downstream of a clog, and someone answered correctly: ischemia — low oxygen, tissue damage and death, and pain.

Trait versus disease

Two trait parents — 25% unaffected, 50% trait, 25% disease, each pregnancy.

DiagnosisGenotypeHemoglobin composition
Sickle cell traitHBB / HBBS — heterozygous40–45% of total hemoglobin is HbS, the remainder HbA (normal adult hemoglobin)
Sickle cell disease (anemia)HBBS / HBBS — homozygous90–100% HbS in the homozygous state, with no HbA present
🩺 Genetically this one is simpler than thalassemia

The contrast was made explicitly. Thalassemia requires counting up to four genes with four clinical grades; sickle cell disease is straightforward homozygous versus heterozygous. Note too that in some countries where the trait is common — Ghana is one example — churches encourage premarital testing, because two carriers face a 25% risk of an affected child with each pregnancy.

Pathophysiology — one polymerization, many organs

The three downstream arms — vaso-occlusion, vasculopathy, and hemolysis.

1

Vaso-occlusion

Sickled cells lodge in the microcirculation → hypoxia, infarction, and necrosis of vital organs, plus severe pain. Produces acute pain, hyposplenism, osteonecrosis, nephropathy, and acute chest syndrome.

2

Vasculopathy and endothelial dysfunction

The disturbed vessel becomes inflamed and the blood becomes hypercoagulable. Put another way: the blood gets jazzed up in the wrong way — little clogs, inflammation, and a clotting system that no longer knows what it is doing.

3

Hemolysis

Cells are torn apart under arterial pressure, releasing free plasma hemoglobin and raising bilirubin. Free hemoglobin inactivates nitric oxide and increases reactive oxygen species, driving pulmonary hypertension, leg ulcers and cerebrovascular disease. Raised bilirubin gives gallstones and jaundice.

The three crises

⚡

Vaso-occlusive (painful) crisis

Repeated episodes of hypoxic injury and infarction, often associated with infection, dehydration or acidosis. Characterized by extreme pain in the abdomen, joints or chest. In infants and toddlers it presents as dactylitis — painful swelling of hands and feet.

🛑

Aplastic crisis

Caused by parvovirus B19 infection of erythroid precursors in the marrow, characterized by cessation of erythropoiesis. The same mechanism as in hereditary spherocytosis — a maximally compensating marrow suddenly switched off.

🫃

Sequestration crisis

Massive sequestration of deformed red cells in the spleen of children with splenomegaly. The spleen abruptly swallows a large fraction of the circulating blood volume, causing a rapid fall in hemoglobin and hypovolemic shock.

🪝 Memory hook — Three crises, three reticulocyte counts

The three crises can look similar at the bedside — a sickle cell patient who is suddenly much sicker and much more anemic. The reticulocyte count separates them fastest:

  • Aplastic crisis → reticulocytes LOW. Production has stopped. Think parvovirus B19.
  • Sequestration crisis → reticulocytes HIGH, spleen suddenly ENORMOUS. The cells are alive, just not in the circulation.
  • Vaso-occlusive crisis → hemoglobin often near baseline. The problem is pain and ischemia, not an acute drop in red cell mass.

Factors that make sickling worse

Sickle cell disease is a whole-body disease — vascular occlusion on the left, chronic hemolysis on the right.

🔑 Three variables control how much sickling happens
  1. The amount of HbS, and what it can partner withHbS polymerizes best with itself and poorly with HbF and HbA. This is the single most important therapeutic lever in the disease — dilute the HbS with anything else and polymerization falls off sharply.
  2. Hemoglobin concentrationThe rate of polymerization depends on how concentrated the hemoglobin is. The higher the HbS concentration, the more likely HbS molecules will polymerize. Dehydration concentrates the cell and makes sickling worse.
  3. pH — acidosisAcidosis reduces the oxygen affinity of hemoglobin (the Bohr effect), which enhances deoxygenation — and deoxygenated HbS is the form that polymerizes. So acidosis increases sickling.
🧠 Why every treatment in this disease is really the same idea

Look at the list of treatments and notice that nearly all of them attack the same variable — the proportion and concentration of HbS:

  • Hydroxyurea raises HbF — and HbS polymerizes poorly with HbF. You are diluting the polymer.
  • Transfusion adds HbA — same idea from the other direction.
  • Intravenous fluids lower hemoglobin concentration inside the cell.
  • Oxygen keeps hemoglobin in the oxygenated conformation, which does not polymerize.
  • Gene therapy either switches HbF back on (Casgevy) or inserts a working beta gene (Lyfgenia).

The number that anchors it: randomized trial evidence shows that keeping HbS below 30% significantly decreases the risk of stroke.

🩺 Exchange transfusion — the arithmetic problem

There is a practical puzzle worth thinking through. If a patient's HbS is 80% and you want it under 30%, you cannot simply transfuse more blood — you would have to give an impossible volume, and you would make them dangerously polycythemic in the attempt.

So you perform an exchange transfusion: remove some of the patient's blood while giving donor blood, which nets a lower HbS percentage without raising total blood volume. It is effective and it is a lifelong commitment.

Treatment

Hydroxyurea

increases HbF

The mainstay disease-modifying drug. The exact mechanism is not fully known, but the cytotoxic hit to the marrow appears to trigger stress erythropoiesis favouring HbF. Same cytotoxicity gives the side effect: myelosuppression.

Pain control

chronic and acute

These patients suffer chronic pain, not only crisis pain. Undertreatment is a well-documented failure of care in this population.

Folic acid

daily

High red cell turnover consumes folate continuously.

Penicillin prophylaxis

daily, in children

A major advance. Children with functional asplenia are highly vulnerable to encapsulated organisms, and infection frequently precipitates a crisis. Prophylaxis plus pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination.

Blood transfusion

acute and chronic

Lowers %HbS and raises oxygen-carrying capacity. Chronic programs prevent stroke.

Oxygen

supportive

Keeps hemoglobin oxygenated and non-polymerizing.

Splenectomy

selected patients

For recurrent sequestration or massive splenomegaly.

Gene therapy

curative intent

Casgevy uses CRISPR/Cas9 to switch off BCL11A, restoring HbF. Lyfgenia uses a lentiviral vector to insert a working beta globin gene. Plus hematopoietic stem cell transplant.

🧬 The first patient in the world

This was told with visible emotion in lecture. The patient on the front page of the New York Times on 21 October 2024 — treated at Children's National Hospital in Washington, DC — was the first person in the world to receive the FDA-approved gene therapy to cure sickle cell disease.

The lecture was careful about the other half of the story: he went through the wringer. Gene therapy still requires chemotherapy ablation, a hospital stay, and a period with no functioning immune system. The closing observation is worth keeping: CRISPR/Cas9 won its Nobel Prize and is already curing people — science has moved remarkably fast.

Malaria, again

Global sickle cell disease prevalence and mortality — sub-Saharan Africa carries most of the burden.

🧬 The same evolutionary bargain as G6PD
  • Sickle cell trait drops malaria mortality by up to 30% — a substantial protective effect.
  • So the mutation is advantageous in the heterozygous state and devastating in the homozygous state. As put in lecture: it is just not when you have it in the homozygous form.
  • Layer the maps and they align: sickle cell prevalence, G6PD deficiency, and endemic malaria occupy the same territory.

There is a harder observation too. Asked how children with sickle cell disease fared there, Ghanaian colleagues answered: if they make it to 5, they'll make it to 10; if they make it to 10, they'll make it to 15. Care has improved since, but delivering advanced treatment in low-resource settings remains a major challenge — and the countries with the highest disease burden have the least access to the blood banking these patients depend on.

Laboratory diagnosis

Hemoglobin electrophoresis — read the bands and the diagnosis is visible directly.

🔑 Reading that gel
  • Normal adult — one strong HbA band.
  • Normal newborn — a prominent HbF band, because the globin switch has not finished.
  • Sickle cell disease — a big HbS band and NO HbA at all. That absence is the diagnosis.
  • Sickle cell trait — both HbA and HbS present. You can see heterozygosity directly.
  • Hb SC disease — a separate hemoglobinopathy, with bands at both HbS and HbC positions.

Sickle cell smear — note that only a minority of the cells are frankly sickled.

Test or findingResult in sickle cell disease
Hemoglobin electrophoresisHbS present, HbA ABSENT
Solubility testPositive for sickled hemoglobin — HbS behaves abnormally in a low-solubility buffer and the solution turns turbid
Blood smearSickle cells, target cells, and Howell-Jolly bodies
Reticulocyte countIncreased — the marrow is compensating
Genetic testingHBB gene
Newborn screening (HPLC or isoelectric focusing)Presence of HbSS — this is how nearly every case is actually found
🩺 Howell-Jolly bodies tell you the spleen is gone

A Howell-Jolly body is a retained fragment of nuclear DNA in a mature red cell. A working spleen removes them, so their presence means the spleen is not functioning.

In sickle cell disease that is expected: repeated infarction destroys the spleen over the first years of life — autosplenectomy. It also explains the infection risk that drives penicillin prophylaxis and vaccination, and why fever in a child with sickle cell disease is an emergency.

Q: A 4-year-old with sickle cell disease presents with fever to 39°C. His parents ask whether they can wait until morning. What is your answer, and what is the pathophysiology behind it?

Answer

No — fever in a child with sickle cell disease is a medical emergency requiring immediate evaluation and empiric antibiotics. Repeated splenic infarction produces functional asplenia (autosplenectomy) within the first few years of life, leaving the child unable to clear encapsulated organisms — Streptococcus pneumoniae above all — and vulnerable to fulminant sepsis within hours. This is why these children receive daily penicillin prophylaxis and pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination. Infection also frequently precipitates a vaso-occlusive or aplastic crisis.

Q: Why does hydroxyurea help in sickle cell disease, and what is its principal toxicity?

Answer

Hydroxyurea increases fetal hemoglobin (HbF). Because HbS polymerizes well with itself but poorly with HbF, raising the HbF fraction dilutes the polymer and reduces sickling, crises and organ damage. The mechanism is thought to involve a cytotoxic hit to the marrow that triggers stress erythropoiesis favouring HbF — and that same cytotoxicity is the principal toxicity: myelosuppression. It is also carcinogenic.

Q: A hemoglobin electrophoresis shows bands at both the HbA and HbS positions, roughly 55% and 43%. Does this patient have sickle cell disease?

Answer

No — this is sickle cell trait. In sickle cell disease the patient is homozygous, so 90–100% of hemoglobin is HbS and there is NO HbA band at all. In trait, HbS makes up 40–45% with the remainder HbA, exactly as shown. Trait is generally asymptomatic — and it confers up to a 30% reduction in malaria mortality, which is why the mutation persists.

Telling Them Apart — Morphology and Laboratory Side by Side

This objective asks you to differentiate hereditary spherocytosis, thalassemia and sickle cell disease on morphology and labs. Here they are in one place, plus G6PD deficiency.

The smear alone often gets you there

Cell you seeWhat it meansFound in
Spherocyte — a ball, no central pallorMembrane has been lost or is structurally defectiveHereditary spherocytosis; autoimmune hemolytic anemia; also G6PD after a bite
Bite cell / blister cell — a semicircular chunk missingA splenic macrophage has removed a Heinz body plus overlying membraneG6PD deficiency
Heinz body — an inclusion (supravital stain)Precipitated, oxidized hemoglobinG6PD deficiency; also thalassemia (precipitated excess chains)

Sickle cell — a rigid crescentPolymerized HbSSickle cell disease
Schistocyte — an angular fragmentMechanical shearingMicroangiopathic hemolytic anemia; mechanical valves; also seen in sickle cell disease

🪝 Memory hook — Match the cell to the culprit
  • Ball → the membrane failed → spherocytosis
  • Bite → an oxidant inclusion was removed → G6PD
  • Bull's-eye → not enough hemoglobin for the membrane → thalassemia
  • Crescent → HbS polymerized → sickle cell
  • Fragment → it was physically shredded → microangiopathic

The full comparison

Hereditary spherocytosisG6PD deficiencyThalassemiaSickle cell disease
DefectMembrane cytoskeletonRed cell enzymeQuantity of globin chainsStructure of the beta chain
InheritanceAutosomal dominantX-linkedAutosomal recessive, gene-dose dependentAutosomal recessive

⚠️ Three microcytic anemias that look alike and are treated completely differently

The commonest real-world error in this whole block. All three give a low mean corpuscular volume:

  • Iron deficiency — ferritin LOW, TIBC HIGH. Give iron.
  • Anemia of chronic disease — ferritin HIGH, TIBC LOW. Treat the underlying disease.
  • Thalassemia trait — ALL iron studies normal, MCV disproportionately low for the mild anemia, red cell count HIGH. Give nothing — and specifically do not give iron.

Give iron to a thalassemic patient and you produce the exact complication you spend the rest of their care chelating out.

🩺 The one test that separates the two spherocytic diseases

Spherocytes appear in both hereditary spherocytosis and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The direct Coombs test (direct antiglobulin test) settles it by asking a single question: are the patient's red cells coated with antibody?

  • Negative → no antibody coating → the defect is intrinsic to the membrane → hereditary spherocytosis.
  • Positive → antibody-coated cells → immune-mediated hemolysis.

This test is covered in detail in the transfusion lecture, where the indirect Coombs test — the photo negative of the same idea — is used to screen a patient's plasma for red cell antibodies before transfusion.

Q: Both hereditary spherocytosis and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia present with anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly and spherocytes on the smear. Name the single test that distinguishes them and explain the logic.

Answer

The direct Coombs test (direct antiglobulin test). It detects antibody bound to the patient's own red cells. In autoimmune hemolytic anemia the cells are antibody-coated, so the test is positive; splenic macrophages remove pieces of the antibody-tagged membrane, which is why spherocytes form. In hereditary spherocytosis the defect is an intrinsic cytoskeletal protein with no antibody involved, so the test is negative. Note that the hereditary spherocytosis case in this file states explicitly that the Coombs test was negative.

Case Review

Three cases from lecture, all inside the increased destruction circle. Commit to an answer before revealing — and in each one, identify which single value settles it.

Case 1 — 13-year-old female

🧍

Presentation

  • Six-month history of generalized weakness, yellowish discoloration of eyes and skin, decreased appetite, exertional breathlessness
  • History of episodic jaundice since early childhood
  • Father had jaundice in adolescence, never formally diagnosed; siblings asymptomatic
  • Exam: mild pallor, moderate jaundice, spleen palpable 6 cm below the costal margin, no hepatomegaly
🧪

Laboratory

  • Hemoglobin 9 g/dL
  • Reticulocyte count 11.45% — markedly raised
  • MCHC 40% — high
  • Smear: spherocytes, anisopoikilocytosis, mild polychromasia
  • Osmotic fragility markedly increased
  • Coombs test NEGATIVE
  • Bilirubin total 5.1 mg/dL (indirect 3.4)
  • Bone marrow: erythroid hyperplasia

Q: What is the diagnosis, which value excludes the main alternative, and how is she managed?

Answer

Hereditary spherocytosis.

The picture is chronic extravascular hemolysis: spherocytes, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, splenomegaly, a high reticulocyte count and erythroid hyperplasia in the marrow. The autosomal dominant inheritance shows in the father's adolescent jaundice. Increased osmotic fragility confirms it — a spherocyte has no spare membrane, so it lyses in hypotonic saline where a normal biconcave disc does not. The high MCHC fits: the cell is smaller for its hemoglobin content.

The value that excludes the alternative is the NEGATIVE Coombs test. Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia also produces spherocytes, jaundice and splenomegaly — but its cells are antibody-coated and the Coombs test would be positive.

Management: folic acid supplementation to support the high-turnover marrow, and splenectomy pending further evaluation — removing the site of destruction normalizes red cell lifespan and removes the rupture risk of a spleen this size. She will need pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination first.

Case 2 — 2-year-old male

🧍

Presentation

  • Progressive pallor and failure to thrive
  • Born full-term without complications; pallor and irritability began around 6 months of age
  • Poor feeding, delayed milestones, increasing abdominal distension
  • First transfusion at 12 months; has required transfusions every 4–6 weeks since
  • An older sibling died at age 3 of an undiagnosed anemia
  • Exam: pale, mildly icteric, frontal bossing and maxillary prominence, liver 3 cm and spleen 6 cm below costal margin, height and weight below the 5th percentile
🧪

Laboratory

  • Hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL
  • MCV 65 fL — microcytic
  • Reticulocyte count 8%
  • Smear: microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells
  • Electrophoresis: markedly reduced HbA, elevated HbF and HbA₂

Q: What is the diagnosis? Explain the age of onset and the facial findings, and give the management.

Answer

Beta thalassemia major.

Why it presented at 6 months and not at birth: a fetus and newborn run on HbF (α₂γ₂), which does not require beta chains. The baby was genuinely well. Only as the globin switch turned gamma off and beta was supposed to take over — at 3 to 6 months — did the deficiency appear. The electrophoresis shows the consequence: reduced HbA with elevated HbF and HbA₂, because he never successfully made the switch.

Why the facial findings: frontal bossing and maxillary prominence come from massive expansion of the marrow cavities in the skull and face, as ineffective erythropoiesis drives the marrow to expand into any available space. Failure to thrive follows from chronic anemia plus the enormous metabolic cost of that drive.

Management: regular packed red cell transfusions every 3–4 weeks; iron chelation with deferasirox — essential, because there is no physiologic route to excrete transfusional iron; folic acid; genetic counseling for the parents (a sibling has already died, and each pregnancy carries a 25% risk); and evaluation for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which along with gene therapy is potentially curative.

Case 3 — 1-year-old male

🧍

Presentation

  • Fever, pallor and irritability — three days of fever to 38.9°C, poor feeding, excessive crying
  • Six months of intermittent joint swelling and abdominal pain
  • Two previous hospitalizations for anemia and pneumonia
  • No known family history of hemoglobinopathies
  • Exam: ill-appearing, irritable, febrile 38.8°C; mild scleral icterus; spleen 4 cm below the costal margin; mild swelling of hands and feet suggestive of dactylitis; growth at the 10th percentile
🧪

Laboratory

  • Hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL
  • White cell count 18,000/µL
  • Reticulocyte count 9%
  • Smear: sickled cells, target cells, anisopoikilocytosis
  • Electrophoresis: HbS 85%, HbF 12%, HbA 0%

Q: What is the diagnosis, what does the electrophoresis prove, and what must be done immediately?

Answer

Sickle cell disease.

What the electrophoresis proves: HbS 85% with HbA 0% means he is homozygous — this is disease, not trait. In trait you would see roughly 40–45% HbS alongside HbA. The residual HbF of 12% is protective, because HbS polymerizes poorly with HbF, and raising it is exactly what hydroxyurea aims to do. Note that his parents had no known family history: sickle cell trait is asymptomatic, so carrier parents frequently do not know.

The immediate priority is the fever, not the anemia. Repeated splenic infarction has left him functionally asplenic, so a febrile child with sickle cell disease can become septic with an encapsulated organism within hours. The dactylitis — painful swelling of hands and feet — is a classic first vaso-occlusive presentation in infants.

Management: Acute: intravenous fluids (dilution reduces sickling), antipyretics, and empiric antibiotics — ceftriaxone without waiting for cultures. Transfusion: packed red cells. Prophylaxis: start daily penicillin and folic acid; ensure pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccines are current. Education: teach the family to recognize vaso-occlusive crisis and infection. Follow-up: referral to a comprehensive pediatric sickle cell program.

Hemolysis — general
Hemolysis
Destruction of red blood cells before the end of their normal ~120-day lifespan.
Intravascular hemolysis
Destruction inside the blood vessel, releasing free hemoglobin into the plasma.
Extravascular hemolysis
Destruction outside the vessel, by macrophages of the spleen and liver.
Haptoglobin
A plasma protein that binds free hemoglobin after intravascular hemolysis. The complex is cleared by the reticuloendothelial system, so serum haptoglobin falls when it is consumed.
Hemopexin
A second scavenger, which binds free heme rather than intact hemoglobin.
Hemoglobinemia
Free hemoglobin in the plasma — the reason plasma appears pink rather than yellow.
Hemoglobinuria
Hemoglobin in the urine, making it dark or tea-coloured. A urine dipstick reads positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy.
Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin
Bilirubin that has not yet been processed by the liver. Raised in all hemolysis, causing jaundice.
RES — reticuloendothelial system
The macrophage network of spleen, liver and bone marrow that clears damaged cells and hemoglobin complexes.
Compensatory erythropoiesis
The marrow's response to peripheral cell loss — a high reticulocyte count and a hypercellular marrow.
Aplastic crisis
A sudden cessation of red cell production, classically caused by parvovirus B19 infecting erythroid precursors.
Cell morphology
Spherocyte
A round, dense red cell with no central pallor. Seen in hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
Bite cell
A red cell with a semicircular defect, where a splenic macrophage removed a Heinz body plus overlying membrane.
Blister cell
The same event with the membrane still stretched over the defect.
Heinz body
An intracellular inclusion of precipitated, oxidized hemoglobin. Requires a supravital stain (crystal violet) to visualize.
Target cell (codocyte)
A red cell with a bull's-eye appearance, from too much membrane relative to hemoglobin content.
Schistocyte
An angular red cell fragment, from mechanical shearing.
Howell-Jolly body
A retained nuclear DNA fragment in a mature red cell. Its presence means the spleen is absent or non-functional.
Anisocytosis
Variation in red cell size.
Poikilocytosis
Variation in red cell shape. Anisopoikilocytosis is both together.
Polychromasia
A bluish tinge on a Wright-stained smear, indicating young reticulocytes with residual RNA.
Biconcave disc
The normal red cell shape — thick at the rim, thin in the middle, giving central pallor and high deformability.
Hereditary spherocytosis
HS
Hereditary spherocytosis. Autosomal dominant defect in a red cell membrane cytoskeletal protein.
Ankyrin, band 3, spectrin, protein 4.2
The cytoskeletal proteins whose defects cause hereditary spherocytosis.
ANK1, SPTB, SLC4A1
The genes tested for hereditary spherocytosis.
Osmotic fragility test
Red cells exposed to hypotonic saline. Spherocytes have no spare membrane and lyse where normal cells do not — increased fragility.
MCHC
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration. Characteristically high in hereditary spherocytosis.
Direct Coombs test (direct antiglobulin test)
Detects antibody coating the patient's own red cells. Negative in hereditary spherocytosis, positive in autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
Pigmented gallstones
Bilirubin stones formed from the chronic heme load of ongoing hemolysis.
Hemosiderosis
Iron overload — here, secondary to repeated transfusion.
G6PD deficiency
G6PD
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase. The red cell's only meaningful source of NADPH.
NADPH
Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (reduced). Powers glutathione reductase.
Glutathione
The antioxidant that, in its reduced form, converts hydrogen peroxide to water.
Oxidant stress
Any exposure generating reactive oxygen species — infection, certain drugs, or fava beans.
G6PD A−
WHO class III variant, seen in about 10% of Black males in the United States. Enzyme half-life ~13 days versus a normal 62 — mild, self-limited hemolysis of older cells.
G6PD Mediterranean
WHO class II variant, prevalent in the Middle East. Half-life measured in hours, so the entire red cell population is vulnerable and hemolysis can be severe.
Favism
Hemolysis triggered by eating fava beans, which generate oxidants when metabolized.
Primaquine, chloroquine, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin
The classic drug triggers.
Thalassemia
Thalassemia
Reduced synthesis of one globin chain, causing low hemoglobin content and destruction from the unpaired partner chain.
Alpha thalassemia
Deficient alpha chain synthesis. Four alpha genes on chromosome 16.
Beta thalassemia
Deficient beta chain synthesis. Two beta genes on chromosome 11.
β⁰ / β⁺
Complete absence of / reduced but not absent beta globin chain production.
Thalassemia minor (trait)
Heterozygous beta thalassemia — one normal beta gene, mild anemia.
Thalassemia major
Homozygous beta thalassemia — severe, transfusion-dependent anemia.
Silent carrier / alpha thalassemia trait
Three / two of four alpha genes present. Asymptomatic, or minimal anemia.
Hemoglobin H disease
One of four alpha genes present. Excess beta chains form β₄ tetramers (HbH), which precipitate and are removed by the spleen — moderately severe anemia.
Hydrops fetalis
No alpha genes. Excess gamma chains form Hb Barts (γ₄), with extremely high oxygen affinity that cannot release oxygen to tissue — intrauterine fetal death.
HbA / HbF / HbA₂
Adult hemoglobin (α₂β₂) / fetal hemoglobin (α₂γ₂) / a minor adult hemoglobin (α₂δ₂), raised in beta thalassemia.
Globin switch
The perinatal transition from gamma to beta chain production. Explains why beta thalassemia and sickle cell disease present at 3–6 months, not at birth.
Ineffective hematopoiesis
Precursors destroyed within the marrow before release — a hypercellular marrow with profound anemia.
Iron chelation
Drug therapy (deferasirox, deferiprone, deferoxamine) to remove transfusional iron, since the body has no route to excrete it.
Frontal bossing / maxillary prominence
Facial changes from massive expansion of skull and facial marrow cavities under extreme erythropoietic drive.
HPLC
High performance liquid chromatography — separates and quantifies hemoglobin species.
Isoelectric focusing
An electrophoretic method separating hemoglobins by isoelectric point; used in newborn screening.
Sickle cell disease
HbS
Sickle hemoglobin. Beta chain with valine substituted for glutamic acid at position 6.
Sickle cell trait
Heterozygous — 40–45% HbS with the remainder HbA. Generally asymptomatic; confers up to 30% reduction in malaria mortality.
Sickle cell disease
Homozygous — 90–100% HbS with no HbA.
Polymerization
Deoxygenated HbS molecules aggregating into rigid fibers that deform and stiffen the cell.
Vaso-occlusive (painful) crisis
Repeated hypoxic injury and infarction from cells lodged in the microvasculature. Severe pain in abdomen, joints or chest.
Sequestration crisis
Massive trapping of red cells in an enlarged spleen, causing rapid anemia and hypovolemia.
Acute chest syndrome
New pulmonary infiltrate with fever and respiratory symptoms. A leading cause of hospitalization and death.
Dactylitis
Painful swelling of hands and feet. Often the first vaso-occlusive presentation in infants.
Autosplenectomy
Progressive splenic infarction leaving the spleen non-functional, with lifelong susceptibility to encapsulated organisms.
Priapism
Prolonged painful erection from vaso-occlusion; a urologic emergency.
Hydroxyurea
A drug that raises fetal hemoglobin, diluting HbS polymerization. Principal toxicity is myelosuppression.
Exchange transfusion
Removing patient blood while giving donor blood, to lower the HbS percentage without raising blood volume.
Casgevy / Lyfgenia
Approved gene therapies. Casgevy uses CRISPR/Cas9 to switch off BCL11A and restore HbF; Lyfgenia uses a lentiviral vector to insert a working beta globin gene.
BCL11A
The transcriptional repressor that silences fetal hemoglobin. Disabling it brings HbF back.
Solubility test
A screening test in which HbS produces turbidity in a low-solubility buffer.
Encapsulated organisms
Bacteria with polysaccharide capsules — pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b — that a functioning spleen is essential for clearing.

🎯 Anemia II — Hemolytic Anemias — High-Yield One-Pager

UNE COM · condensed by learning objective — hemolysis type · membrane and enzyme defects · globin chain disorders

Hemolysis · LO 1

The three shared features

  • Shortened red cell lifespan (normal ~120 days).
  • Accumulation of hemoglobin catabolism products — unconjugated bilirubin → jaundice.
  • Compensatory erythropoiesis → reticulocytes HIGH, hypercellular marrow. This is the split from Part 1.

Intravascular

  • Schistocytes (sometimes)
  • Hemoglobinemia — plasma pink, not yellow
  • Hemoglobinuria — dipstick positive, no RBCs on microscopy
  • Jaundice (unconjugated)
  • Haptoglobin decreased or ABSENT
  • Kidney at risk — free heme is nephrotoxic. Worse than extravascular.

Extravascular

  • Spherocytes
  • Haptoglobin decreased, mildly
  • Jaundice (unconjugated)
  • Splenomegaly
  • No hemoglobinemia or hemoglobinuria

Haptoglobin

  • Plasma protein that binds free hemoglobin.
  • Complex cleared by the reticuloendothelial system → serum level falls.
  • A consumption marker: low = the mop has been used.
Membrane & enzyme · LO 2–3

Hereditary spherocytosis

  • Autosomal dominant; membrane cytoskeleton defect.
  • Proteins: ankyrin, band 3, α/β spectrin, protein 4.2. Genes ANK1, SPTB, SLC4A1.
  • Sphere = less deformable → splenic (extravascular) destruction.
  • Anemia · jaundice · splenomegaly · pigmented gallstones; high MCHC; hypercellular marrow.
  • Hemolytic crisis (infection) and aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19).
  • Dx: spherocytes, osmotic fragility INCREASED, retics high, Coombs NEGATIVE.
  • Tx: folic acid, transfusion, splenectomy (vaccinate first).

G6PD deficiency

  • X-linked; world's most common enzyme deficiency, >400 million.
  • Enzyme made in normal amounts but unstable → deficient in OLDER cells only.
  • G6PD → NADPH → glutathione reductase → reduced glutathione → H₂O₂ → water.
  • Without it: H₂O₂ oxidizes hemoglobin → Heinz bodies → spleen bites → bite & blister cells.
  • Triggers: infection (commonest), drugs (primaquine, chloroquine, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin), fava beans.
  • Class III = G6PD A−, 10% US Black males, half-life 13 d → mild, self-limited. Class II = Mediterranean, half-life hours → severe.
  • Assay can be falsely NORMAL during a crisis — repeat at 2–3 months.
  • Malaria protection; distribution matches endemic malaria.
Globin chains · LO 2, 4

Thalassemia — framework

  • 4 alpha genes (chr 16), 2 beta genes (chr 11). HbA = α₂β₂.
  • Low hemoglobin → hypochromia, microcytosis.
  • Excess unpartnered chain aggregates → precursor death in marrow (ineffective hematopoiesis) + splenic lysis.
  • Globin switch: HbF α₂γ₂ prenatal → HbA α₂β₂ postnatal. Explains onset at 3–6 months.
  • HbH = β₄; Hb Barts = γ₄ (extremely high O₂ affinity, cannot deliver).

Alpha & beta grades

  • 3/4 genes = silent carrier — asymptomatic.
  • 2/4 = alpha trait — minimal anemia, normal iron studies.
  • 1/4 = hemoglobin H disease — moderately severe.
  • 0/4 = hydrops fetalis — Hb Barts, intrauterine fetal death.
  • β⁰ = no beta chains; β⁺ = reduced.
  • Minor/trait = heterozygous, mild. Major = homozygous, transfusion dependent.

Thalassemia dx & tx

  • Smear: target cells, hypochromia, anisopoikilocytosis, Heinz bodies, nucleated RBCs.
  • Electrophoresis/HPLC: enlarged HbF band, raised HbA₂. Genes HBA1, HBB.
  • Iron studies normal (or high if transfused) — do NOT give iron.
  • Newborn screening is how it is found.
  • Tx: transfusion + iron chelation + folate; gene therapy / stem cell transplant.
  • Frontal bossing = marrow cavity expansion.

Sickle cell disease

  • Point mutation, HBB: valine for glutamic acid at position 6 → HbS.
  • Trait = 40–45% HbS + HbA. Disease = 90–100% HbS, NO HbA.
  • Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes → rigid sickle cell → vaso-occlusion → ischemia, infarction, pain.
  • Crises: vaso-occlusive (Hgb at baseline) · aplastic (parvovirus, retics LOW) · sequestration (spleen huge, retics high).
  • Worse with: high HbS%, dehydration, acidosis. HbS polymerizes poorly with HbF and HbA.
  • Tx: hydroxyurea (↑HbF), penicillin prophylaxis + vaccines, folate, transfusion/exchange to keep HbS <30%, oxygen, pain control; Casgevy / Lyfgenia, transplant.
  • Dx: HbS present, HbA absent; solubility positive; sickle cells, target cells, Howell-Jolly bodies; newborn screen.
  • Fever = emergency (autosplenectomy). Trait drops malaria mortality up to 30%.
